Monkey indices

Source: R/monkey_indices.R
monkey_indices.Rd

Twelve summary statistics of a pairwise genome alignment that were not designed to represent a biological fact. They were retained from a screen of 5,420 functions assembled mechanically from the columns of the alignment table and from generic descriptive statistics ("monkey typing"), for the following properties on 1,910 alignments of 16 clades: reproducible between the alignment of A to B and the alignment of B to A, more alike between genome pairs that share an ancestor than between random pairs, different from the value obtained after shuffling the order and the strand of the alignments, and not strongly correlated with the statistics that already existed in this package, nor with each other (absolute rank correlation below 0.6). Their biological meaning, if any, is to be found. Each function is named after a famous monkey.

Usage

wukong_index(gb)

abu_index(gb)

albert_index(gb)

marcel_index(gb)

imo_index(gb)

rafiki_index(gb)

hanuman_index(gb)

jack_index(gb)

able_index(gb)

mizaru_index(gb)

george_index(gb)

baker_index(gb)

Arguments

gb

A GBreaks object, not coalesced, in which all ranges are on the + or - strand.

Value

A numeric value, or NA when it can not be computed: fewer than three values, or no variation.

Details

All the functions take the alignments as loaded and sort them on the target genome. mizaru_index() then coalesces them with coalesce_contigs and its default arguments; the others use them as they are. They use the following quantities.

  • A junction is a pair of consecutive alignments on the same target sequence. A same-query junction is a junction whose two alignments are also on the same query sequence.

  • The target gap of a junction is the number of bases between its two alignments on the target genome, plus one; the query gap of a same-query junction is the same on the query genome, whatever the order and the strand of the two alignments.

  • The gap contrast of a same-query junction is \((t - q) / (t + q)\) where \(t\) and \(q\) are its target gap and its query gap. It is positive when the two alignments are further apart on the target.

  • The rank step of a same-query junction is the number of positions between its two alignments in the order of the alignments on the query genome (1 for neighbours), and its direction is +1 when the two alignments are on the same strand and follow each other on the query as that strand implies, -1 when they follow each other in the opposite direction, and 0 when they are on opposite strands.

  • The edge distance of an alignment on a genome is the distance from its centre to the nearest end of the sequence, divided by half the length of the sequence: 0 at the ends, 1 in the middle. The relative position is the position of the centre from 0 (first base) to 1 (last base).

  • Sizes (widths, gaps, rank steps) are used on the logarithmic scale.

The functions are the following. The monkey is introduced first.

wukong_index()

Sun Wukong: the Monkey King of the Chinese novel Journey to the West. Tail weight of the query gaps: on the logarithmic scale, range between the 10th and the 90th percentiles divided by the interquartile range.

abu_index()

Abu: kleptomaniac pet monkey of the street thief in the Aladdin films. Quartile skewness of the gap contrasts: \((Q_3 + Q_1 - 2 Q_2) / (Q_3 - Q_1)\).

albert_index()

Albert II: rhesus macaque, first primate to reach space, in 1949. Excess kurtosis of the gap contrasts.

marcel_index()

Marcel: white-headed capuchin kept by Ross in the sitcom Friends. Standard deviation of the absolute difference between the relative positions of an alignment on the two genomes. The query position is counted from the other end of the sequence when most aligned bases between the two sequences are on the minus strand.

imo_index()

Imo: Japanese macaque of Koshima who started washing sweet potatoes. Correlation between the edge distance of an alignment on the target genome and the edge distance of its neighbours on the query genome. Neighbours are the alignments before and after it on the same target sequence; the two members of a junction are exchangeable.

rafiki_index()

Rafiki: mandrill shaman who presents the newborn cub in The Lion King. Rank correlation, over same-query junctions, between the query gap and the mean edge distance of the two alignments on the query genome.

hanuman_index()

Hanuman: monkey-faced Hindu deity, devoted companion of Rama in the Ramayana. Rank correlation, over junctions, between the mean width of the two alignments and the absolute difference of their edge distances on the query genome.

jack_index()

Jack: chacma baboon who operated railway signals in South Africa in the 1880s. Rank correlation, over same-query junctions, between the rank step and the direction.

able_index()

Able: rhesus macaque, Miss Baker's companion on the 1959 spaceflight. Correlation, over same-query junctions, between the rank step and the absolute difference of the edge distances of the two alignments on the query genome.

mizaru_index()

Mizaru: the see-no-evil monkey carved at the Toshogu shrine in Nikko. Rank correlation, over the junctions of the coalesced alignments, between the target gap and the absolute difference of the edge distances of the two coalesced alignments on the query genome.

george_index()

Curious George: inquisitive little monkey of the children's books by the Reys. Correlation, over junctions, between the target gap and the mean score per aligned column of the two alignments. Stops with an error without the score and aLength metadata columns.

baker_index()

Miss Baker: squirrel monkey who survived a suborbital spaceflight in 1959. Correlation, weighted by the width of the alignments on the target genome, between the number of gap openings per aligned column of an alignment and the geometric mean of the target gaps of the junctions that flank it. Stops with an error without the gapOpens and aLength metadata columns.

Ranks are computed within each vector before restricting it to the junctions used: in rafiki_index(), the mean edge distances are ranked among all junctions. Variances are population variances. Quantiles are those of stats::quantile with default settings.

The results do not depend on the order of the sequences nor on their orientation: reversing a sequence with reverse does not change them. They are not symmetric: the value on swap(gb) differs. Note that swap drops the metadata columns that george_index() and baker_index() need.

The functions that use edge distances or relative positions need sequence lengths. Missing lengths are replaced by the end of the last alignment of each sequence, with forceSeqLengths.

See also

The vignette vignette("MonkeyIndices", package = "GenomicBreaks") reports how the functions were selected and how they behave on the alignments of the screen. The code of the screen is in system.file("scripts", "monkey_screen", package = "GenomicBreaks").

Author

Claude (Anthropic), from a screen requested by Charles Plessy.

Examples

# Alignment of two yeast genomes
gb <- load_genomic_breaks(
  system.file("extdata/SacCer3__SacPar.gff3.gz", package = "GenomicBreaks"))
wukong_index(gb)
#> [1] 2.496076
abu_index(gb)
#> [1] 0.1227582
albert_index(gb)
#> [1] -1.082118
marcel_index(gb)
#> [1] 0.1281138
imo_index(gb)
#> [1] 0.9163483
rafiki_index(gb)
#> [1] 0.03985051
hanuman_index(gb)
#> [1] 0.5777603
jack_index(gb)
#> [1] -0.5166595
able_index(gb)
#> [1] 0.2710925
mizaru_index(gb)
#> [1] 0.007696371

# The orientation of the sequences does not matter.
marcel_index(reverse(forceSeqLengths(gb)))
#> [1] 0.1281138

# The GFF3 format does not record the alignment length nor the number of gap
# openings, which the blasttab+ format does.  Lower bounds are used here
# for illustration.
gb$aLength  <- pmax(width(gb), width(gb$query))
gb$gapOpens <- as.integer(width(gb) != width(gb$query))
george_index(gb)
#> [1] 0.1178123
baker_index(gb)
#> [1] -0.01414999
